newsitem.title: USA: U.S. warns Taiwan, China on excercises.
newsitem.headline: U.S. warns Taiwan, China on excercises.

text.p: The United States has warned Taiwan and China against staging military exercises during the sensitive runup to Hong Kong's return July 1 to Chinese control.

"It's best to stand down in times like this and to continue activities that promote goodwill and understanding and peace and not to engage in activtiies that are counterproductive," State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns told reporters.
"We've been concerned enough about the reports (that Taiwan and China would stage military exercises this month) that we of course urged this (restraint) upon the governments," he said.

Taiwan announced major military exercises for June 23-24 and an independent Hong Kong newspaper reported on Tuesday that China is planning to respond with its own military exercises sometime this month.
If both governments go ahead with war games, tensions could return to March 1996 levels when China shook the region with live-fire exercises in the Taiwan Straits off Taiwan.

China said then it was warning voters in Taiwan's first presidential elections against any moves toward declaring independence. Washington responded by sending two aircraft carrier battle groups to the region in support for Taiwan.
Burns said Washington was encouraged by the gradual easing of tensions in the Taiwan Straits region since then.

"And we hope China and Taiwan will continue their efforts to reduce tensions between them to make the Taiwan Straits a region of peace that includes restraint in military activities. This is a sensitive area at a sensitive time."
"We're making it very clear today that we think the gerneral good trend in the Taiwan Straits ought to be continued by both governments," Burns said.

Despite the U.S. warning, Taiwan's chief representative in Washington said on Wednesday U.S. officials "fully understand" Taiwan's plan to stage war games on the eve of Hong Kong's reversion from British colony to Chinese control.
Jason Hu of the office that functions as an embassy in the absence of U.S.-Taiwanese diplomatic relations acknowledged Washington raised questions about the exercises.
After Taiwan responded to U.S. concerns, "we all fully understand," Hu told reporters at the National Press Club. He declined to elaborate.
China regards Taiwan as a renegade province because it was a refuge for Nationalist troops who lost China's civil war to the communists in 1949.
Hu, who heads the Taipei Economic and Cultural Representative Office, said the timing of the exercise was unrelated to the Hong Kong handover at midnight on June 30.

"There's no political message, period," he said, describing the war games as routine and long-delayed. Pressed on the timing, he said there was "no better time" because political significance could always be imputed.

In strongly worded opening remarks, Hu drew sharp distinctions between Hong Kong's situation and any future reunification of Taiwan and China. He said Hong Kong had to accept the "one country, two systems" formula promised by Beijing in the absence of any viable alternatives.
"But Taiwan does have an alternative: it has the power to say 'no' to immediate annexation and to maintain its continuing democracy, freedom and prosperity," he said.
On the bright side, he said Hong Kong may ultimately serve as a "practical neutral ground of sorts that might lessen Beijing's allergy to the growth of democracy" on its soil.

Vowing to pursue "pragmatic diplomacy" despite Beijing's objections, Hu said Taiwan was not trying to "poke sticks in the gorilla's cage," adding: "We cannot do enough to stay out of trouble ourselves and we do not wish to cause trouble for anyone ... What we do, we do for survival's sake."
